MULCH: Mulch is a covering laid over garden soil. Bark chips are one kind, but the word describes the covering's use rather than a single material.
WHEEL: A wheel rotates around an axle. Its tire is an outer covering, not another name for the entire wheel.
LOAD: A load is the material being carried. The wheelbarrow or cart is the vehicle supporting that load.
PATH: A path is a route for walking. Stepping stones can mark that route without making a continuous paved surface.
STONE: Stone is a piece of natural rock. A slab is a relatively flat piece, while gravel consists of many smaller pieces.
STEP: Step can name an action or one level of a stairway. In a stepping-stone clue, it concerns placing a foot on the next surface.
BARREL: A barrel is a large rounded container. A rain barrel collects runoff; its tap lets water leave without lifting the whole container.
TAP: Tap can mean a faucet or a light knock. The water-container scene uses the faucet meaning.
PUMP: A pump moves liquid. A faucet or tap controls the opening through which the liquid comes out.
POOL: Pool can name swimming water or a small area collected in a hollow. A tide pool remains among shore rocks as the sea level falls.
SWIM: Swimming uses the body to move through water. Floating means remaining supported at the surface without necessarily traveling.
PEBBLE: A pebble is a small stone. Moving water can round its edges over time, giving a brook pebble its smooth shape.
STREAM: A stream is flowing water in a channel. Brook and creek are other common words for small natural waterways.
CHEESE: Cheese comes in many textures and flavors. Sharp describes flavor, while a wedge describes the shape of a cut portion.
WEDGE: A wedge narrows toward one edge or point. A lemon wedge and a cheese wedge share that shape but are different foods.
COUNTER: A counter is a raised work or serving surface. In a shop it separates the customer area from the worker's space.
SCALE: A scale measures weight. Its reading is different from a price, although a shop may calculate price using that weight.
WRAP: Wrap means put a covering around something. Paper is common for parcels and shop goods, while cloth can also be a wrapping material.
RECEIPT: A receipt records a completed payment. A bill asks for payment, so the two papers serve different purposes.
ADDRESS: An address tells where mail should go. The recipient's name identifies the person, while the street, city, and postal code locate the destination.
HARDWARE: A hardware store sells tools and practical supplies. A key blank can be cut there to match the shape of an existing key.
LOCK: A lock restricts access until the correct key or code is used. A latch holds a door closed without necessarily locking it.
METAL: Metal names a family of materials including iron, copper, and aluminum. The word does not identify which metal a particular tool contains.
PARCEL: A parcel is a wrapped package prepared for delivery. Labeling and secure wrapping help keep its address and contents together.
LABEL: A label identifies an item or its contents. It can carry a name, date, size, or address depending on the scene.
TAPE: Adhesive tape fastens surfaces with a sticky strip. Magnetic recording tape is a different material sharing the same short name.
TOWN: A town is a community. Its square or town hall is only one place within the larger community.
HALL: Hall can mean an entrance passage or a large gathering room. A town hall is a public building, while a hallway is a passage.
FOUNTAIN: A fountain moves water through a spray or stream. The basin catches the water; it is one part of the whole structure.
BASIN: A basin is an open container or depression holding water. In a garden fixture, it is the broad bowl below the spray or drinking rim.
FOLDER: A folder groups loose papers without binding them into a book. A label on its tab helps the stored pages be found again.
FILE: File can mean an organized collection or the act of putting papers away. In a desk scene, it is not the rough metal tool used in a workshop.
DRAWER: A drawer slides in and out of furniture. Its front may have a handle, while dividers separate the contents inside.
MIRROR: A mirror reflects light to form an image. Cleaning the surface removes marks; it does not change the reflected object.
GLASS: Glass is usually transparent but can also be colored. A glass is a drinking vessel, while glass without an article can name the material.
LEVEL: A level checks whether a surface is horizontal or vertical. It helps a frame hang straight without judging by sight alone.
POINT: Point names a tapered end. A sharpened pencil needs a usable point, while a worn one makes a broader mark.
ERASER: An eraser removes many graphite marks by rubbing them from the paper. It does not work the same way on every kind of ink.
HANGER: A hanger supports a garment by its shoulders. A hook can hold the hanger or directly hold a coat, depending on the entryway.
BUTTON: A button fastens through a buttonhole or loop. Some have holes through the face; others attach by a small shank on the back.
SHIRT: A shirt has separate parts such as a collar, sleeves, and cuffs. Naming the part helps distinguish it from the whole garment.
BATH: Bath can mean washing the body or the water prepared for it. The tub is the container rather than the washing activity.
SOAP: Soap helps remove dirt when used with water. Rinsing carries away the loosened dirt and remaining suds.
TOWEL: Towels absorb water after washing or swimming. Their looped fabric holds more moisture than a smooth hard surface.
LACE: A shoelace threads through openings to fasten a shoe. Lace can also name decorative openwork fabric, a different sense.
SOLE: The sole is the shoe's bottom. The tread is the pattern on its outer surface that contacts the ground.
FOOT: A foot is a body part and also a unit of length. A shoe clue points to the body meaning rather than twelve inches.
CROSSWALK: A crosswalk is a marked place to cross a road. The signal gives instructions; the striped crossing itself does not control traffic.
SIGNAL: A signal communicates an instruction. At a crossing it can use lights or symbols rather than spoken words.
CURB: A curb is the raised edge between roadway and sidewalk. The corner is where streets meet, not another name for that raised edge.
STOP: Stop asks for movement to end. At a crossing, it concerns waiting for the appropriate signal rather than a kind of destination.
STREET: A street is a road through a built-up area. Its name and building numbers form part of a postal address.
METER: A parking meter records paid parking time. Meter can also name other measuring devices, so the street scene supplies the intended meaning.
GAS: Gas is the usual American short name for gasoline. The pump sells a liquid fuel despite the short word's other meaning.
HOSE: A hose is a flexible tube. A nozzle shapes the flow at one end, while a tap controls its supply at the other.
FUEL: Fuel provides energy when an engine or heater uses it. Gasoline is one fuel; the general word does not mean gasoline alone.
DASHBOARD: A dashboard places instruments and controls in front of the driver. Gauges display information rather than doing the steering.
SIGN: Sign can be a public notice or the action of writing a name. Check whether the clue describes an object or asks for a verb.
PHONE: Phone is the everyday short form of telephone. Older sets had dials and receivers; newer ones can also show video.
CALL: Call can mean telephone contact or saying a name aloud. Both uses involve trying to get someone's attention.
HELLO: Hello is a greeting. It commonly opens a phone call, while goodbye marks the ending.
NUMBER: A number can count an amount or identify something. A telephone number identifies a connection rather than measuring its size.
LISTEN: Listen means pay attention to a sound. Hearing a sound can happen without deliberately listening to it.
VOICE: A voice is the sound produced when someone speaks or sings. A speaker is the device that reproduces the sound on a call or recording.
SCREEN: Screen can mean a display surface or a mesh barrier. The phone and movie scenes use the display meaning; a porch door uses the mesh meaning.
CAMERA: A camera records pictures. Its lens focuses the scene, while a shutter or electronic control determines when light is recorded.
SPEAKER: A speaker can be a person talking or an audio device. In a video call's controls, it is the device that makes sound audible.
MUTE: Muting stops a microphone from sending sound. It does not necessarily turn off the camera or end a video call.
CART: A cart carries a load on wheels. A grocery cart's basket holds the food while its handle guides the movement.
GROCERY: Grocery describes food and household shopping. A list records intended purchases; the bags contain what was actually bought.
LIST: A list records items in order. Checking off a purchased item is different from changing the price or quantity of it.
ITEM: An item is one entry or object in a group. The same list can include individual foods, packages, and other household supplies.
SIZE: Size describes how big something is. A unit price compares cost for the same quantity, helping when package sizes differ.
CHANGE: Change is the money returned when payment exceeds the price. The word can include several coins rather than just one.
DIME: A U.S. dime is worth ten cents. Two nickels have the same value, although they are different coins.
QUARTER: A U.S. quarter is worth twenty-five cents. Four quarters make one dollar.
CASH: Cash means physical money such as bills and coins. A check gives an instruction to transfer money rather than being cash itself.
DOLLAR: One U.S. dollar equals one hundred cents. Its value can be represented by one bill or several different combinations of coins.
TICKET: A ticket can give admission or identify an item left for a service. A theater ticket and a dry-cleaning claim ticket serve different uses.
USHER: An usher helps people find seats. The role differs from the performers on stage or the clerk selling tickets.
AISLE: An aisle is a passage between rows. In a theater it lets people reach seats without climbing over them.
SHALLOW: Shallow means not deep. At a pool, the word describes the water's depth rather than its temperature.
LOCKER: A locker is a small storage compartment that can be secured. It holds belongings while a visitor uses a pool or activity room.
BUS: A bus carries several passengers on roads. Its route tells where it goes, while its timetable tells when it is scheduled.
SHELTER: A bus shelter protects waiting passengers from some weather. It does not replace checking the route or arrival information.
BENCH: A bench normally seats more than one person. It can be used in a park, entryway, or bus shelter without changing that basic meaning.
ROUTE: A route is a planned course. Several roads or stops can be parts of a single route.
FARE: Fare is the price of a journey. A ticket is the record or pass obtained when that fare is paid.
HAND: Hand can name a body part or a clock pointer. A clock's minute hand makes a full turn each hour.
FACE: Face can name the front of a head or the marked surface of a clock. The surrounding objects identify the sense used in the clue.
DIAL: A dial can show numbers on a clock, telephone, or radio. Its marks identify times, phone choices, or station frequencies according to the object.
WATCH: Watch can be a wrist timepiece or the action of looking attentively. A football-viewing scene uses the action rather than the object.
BAND: Band can mean a strap or a group of musicians. A watch scene uses the strap meaning; an outdoor concert uses the musical group.
WRIST: The wrist joins the hand to the forearm. A wristwatch's strap goes around this joint rather than around the fingers.
BUCKLE: A buckle fastens a belt or strap. Its pin can fit into different holes to adjust the length.
PORCH: A porch is an outdoor entrance area, often with a roof. A patio is usually a paved sitting area at ground level.
CHAIN: A chain is made from connected links. On a porch swing it provides support; on a bicycle it transfers motion.
ACE: An ace is a playing card marked with A. Its value depends on the rules of the game being played.
SUIT: Suit can mean matching clothes or a group of playing cards. Hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades are the four card suits.
DECK: Deck can mean a pack of playing cards or an outdoor platform. Cards and a patio use different senses of the same short word.
DOMINO: A domino tile has two marked ends. A double has the same count on both ends.
DOT: Dot is the everyday word for a small round mark. On dominoes, the groups of dots indicate each end's value.
LINE: Line can mean a row, a drawn mark, or a fishing cord. The clue's action helps distinguish those meanings.
HOOK: A fishing hook catches by its pointed curve. A wall hook is shaped for hanging objects rather than catching fish.
REEL: A reel stores a long flexible strip or line. A fishing reel takes up line, while a film reel holds a strip of images.
CHALK: Chalk leaves a powdery mark that can be wiped away. It is useful on a board or pavement but does not behave like permanent ink.
BLACKBOARD: A blackboard is a writing surface used with chalk. Boards can be dark green as well as black despite the traditional name.
TEACHER: A teacher guides learning. A class is the group of learners or the lesson session, not the teacher's job title.
BELL: A bell rings when a clapper or striker vibrates it. A school bell and a decorative handbell use that same basic sound-making idea.
RECESS: Recess is a break in the school day. The word here concerns time for play rather than the end of the whole school term.
SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
GRADE: A grade records performance in schoolwork. Report cards can use letters, numbers, or written comments depending on the school.
REPORT: A school report summarizes progress. It may include several subjects rather than a single assignment's mark.
TERM: A term is part of a school year. Its length depends on the school's calendar.
NICKEL: A U.S. nickel is worth five cents. The name does not mean the entire coin is made of pure nickel.
FILM: Film can mean the strip used to record pictures or the finished movie. A projector moves the strip to display successive images.
PIANO: A piano sounds when keys cause hammers to strike strings. In silent-film theaters, a live pianist sometimes supplied the accompaniment.
RECEIVER: An older telephone receiver combined the parts for hearing and speaking. Returning it to its cradle ended the call.
CORD: A cord can carry electricity or connect equipment. In an older telephone, the coiled cord let the handset move away from the base.
COMB: A comb has a row of teeth used to arrange hair. A brush uses bristles rather than a single row of rigid teeth.
POLE: A barber pole's stripes traditionally identify the shop. The moving pattern can make the stripes appear to travel upward or downward.
HOME: Home can mean a dwelling or the local side in a sporting match. Read the clue before applying the familiar household meaning.
BALL: A ball is usually round in games such as baseball. American football uses a different, elongated shape.
GAME: Game names the organized activity or contest. Equipment such as a bat or board is used in the game but is not the game itself.
TEAM: A team is a group playing together. In a home-and-away matchup, the home side plays at its own usual venue.
STRIKE: In baseball, a strike can result from a swing and miss. Three strikes normally put the batter out, though foul-ball rules add detail.
DAISY: A daisy is a flower with a familiar bright center and raylike outer parts. Daisy is also the name in the bicycle song Daisy Bell.
BICYCLE: A bicycle has two wheels and is driven by pedals. A tandem is a bicycle designed for riders seated one behind another.
STRING: String is a thin cord used for tying or flying a kite. A kite's string connects the flying frame to the person holding it.
BRICK: A brick is a rectangular building block. In The Wizard of Oz, the yellow road is made from these blocks.
YELLOW: Yellow is a color name rather than a material. The movie's yellow brick road combines a color with a building block.
RADIO: A radio receives broadcasts. Choosing a station selects a particular transmission rather than changing the recorded song itself.
TELEVISION: Early television sets often had tuning knobs and antennas. The particular design varied, so the scene is one example of home viewing.
ANTENNA: A broadcast antenna receives radio waves. Rabbit ears is a familiar nickname for a pair of adjustable indoor television rods.
CHANNEL: A television channel identifies a broadcast choice. Turning the volume changes loudness rather than choosing a different channel.
KNOB: A knob is a rounded control or handle. On an older television it may turn a setting; on a door it may operate a latch.
MARBLE: A playing marble is a small hard ball, often glass. The name here does not refer to the stone used for countertops.
CIRCLE: A circle is a round line or shape. In a marble game, a drawn circle can mark the playing area.
AIM: Aim means direct something toward a target. It is an action, unlike the target or the object being thrown.
HOP: Hopping uses a springing jump. In hopscotch, the grid determines which spaces are used for one foot or two.
HOPSCOTCH: Hopscotch uses a numbered ground pattern and a small marker. Local versions differ, so the puzzle focuses on its familiar equipment and actions.
BOUNCE: A bounce is the return movement after striking a surface. A rubber ball's springiness lets it rise after hitting the floor.
RUBBER: Rubber bends and springs back. That makes it useful for balls and tires as well as waterproof footwear.
JACKS: Jacks are small game pieces, often metal. Players pick them up between bounces of a ball, with the required count increasing by round.
TOP: A toy top spins on a point. Top can also mean the highest part of an object, so the action in the clue matters.
SPIN: Spin means rotate around a center. A top stays upright while turning quickly, then wobbles as it slows.
PARENT: A parent is a mother or father. Family stories and trees can include parents by birth, adoption, or other family relationships.
GRAIN: Grain can mean an edible seed or the pattern of wood fibers. The food and woodworking scenes use different senses of the same word.
LAW: A law is a rule with authority. In the Moses scene, the word concerns commands in the story rather than modern traffic rules.
TEN: Ten is the number associated with the commandments. The puzzle uses the familiar count, not memorization of their order.
KING: King can mean a ruler or a face card representing one. In a card deck, it belongs to a suit rather than ruling a country.
WISDOM: Wisdom is sound judgment, more than simply knowing many facts. Solomon's request concerns the ability to judge his people's cases.
DEN: A den is an animal's sheltered place. In Daniel's story it names the enclosure holding the lions.
ANGEL: Angel means a heavenly messenger in the Bible stories. Decorative angel figures are representations rather than the story characters themselves.
LOST: Lost describes what cannot currently be found. The three Luke 15 parables use different missing things to tell related stories of return and joy.
SHARE: Share means give part of something to others. In a meal setting it can concern food rather than dividing property or money.
THANKS: Thanks expresses gratitude. The feeding story includes giving thanks before food is distributed.
GLOVE: A glove has separate spaces for the fingers. A mitten groups the fingers together and has a separate space for the thumb.
BASEBALL: Baseball uses a bat, ball, and gloves. Its field and equipment clues concern the sport rather than professional-player trivia.
MITT: A mitt is a catching glove with joined finger sections. It is related to but not identical with an ordinary five-finger glove.
SWING: Swing can name a hanging seat or the action of moving a bat. The porch and ballpark settings point to different meanings.
ZOO: A zoo displays and cares for animals. A keeper is a person responsible for animal care, not the name of an enclosure.
TENT: A tent is a portable shelter made from fabric and supports. Its poles hold the shape while pegs or other anchors secure it.
FLAG: A flag can be a cloth symbol or a small signaling marker. A mailbox flag shows a postal signal rather than identifying a country.
JULY: July is the seventh month. The Fourth of July is the U.S. Independence Day holiday.
HOT: Hot describes temperature. A hot dog is a food name, so the two-word phrase has a meaning beyond the adjective alone.
WAGON: A wagon carries people or goods on wheels. A hayride uses the vehicle for an outing, with straw or hay providing the familiar farm setting.
BOOT: A boot rises above the ankle. Its sole can leave a tread pattern in mud or snow.
PRINT: A print can be an image or an impression. In snow, it is the mark left by a foot or shoe rather than words on paper.
CANDLE: A candle burns fuel from its wax through a wick. Its flame produces light as the warmed wax is consumed.
WAX: Wax can form a candle or a protective coating. A candle consumes it as fuel, while polishing leaves a thin layer on a surface.
FLAME: A flame is the visible burning region above fuel. A glowing ember is hot too, but it does not necessarily have a flame.
CAROL: A carol is a seasonal song. In these Christmas scenes it concerns singing rather than a person's name.
SHEET: Sheet can name paper, bed linen, or a flat baking pan. The scene tells whether the material is paper, cloth, or metal.
FOOTBALL: American football uses an oval ball and teams playing toward end zones. The puzzle concerns equipment and watching, not detailed rule recall.
SCORE: A score records points earned. It is different from the game clock, which shows time remaining.
PASS: A pass sends the football to another player. In an entryway or theater, the same word can instead mean permission to enter.
FIELD: A field can be open farmland or a sports playing area. The Thanksgiving game scene uses the sports meaning.
TV: TV is the common abbreviation for television. It is used in descriptions, but the crossword's answers use at least three letters.
MOTHER: Mother names a female parent. In a story scene, the surrounding names help show which family relationship is being described.
SON: Son names a male child in a family. The same word applies to the relationship when the child has grown into an adult.
STAR: A star can mean a distant sun or a pointed decorative shape. Christmas ornaments represent the shape rather than an actual celestial object.
BREAD: Bread may be a whole loaf or pieces cut from it. A loaf is counted as a whole, while a slice is one flat portion.
COIN: A coin is a metal piece of money. The value depends on the currency and period; Bible stories do not use modern U.S. coins.
DONKEY: A donkey is a long-eared working animal. A young donkey can be called a foal or colt; mule names a different animal with donkey and horse parents.
TAIL: Tail can name the rear part of an animal or a trailing end of ribbon or a kite. The word describes different things with a similar extending position.
WING: Wings help birds, many insects, and airplanes fly, but their structures differ. The model-airplane scene uses a fixed surface rather than feathers.
WIND: Wind has two pronunciations and meanings: moving air, or turning something around a center. A yarn ball or clock uses the turning action.
CARD: Card can mean a printed greeting or a playing piece. An envelope points to a greeting; a deck or suit points to a game.
STAMP: Stamp can mean a postage label or a tool that leaves an ink impression. A mailed letter and a craft project use different senses.
